architecture.mechanism: Parasitic redox reactions at the electrode-electrolyte interface drive SEI growth and electrolyte conductivity loss, following Arrhenius and Tafel kinetics, with elevated temperature (e.g., 55 °C) and high SOC (e.g., 90%) synergistically accelerating SEI thickening beyond 300 nm and conductivity loss over 20% during calendar aging.
architecture.intervention: Cap cell storage SOC at a lower level (e.g., 50–70% rather than 90%) in hot-climate grid-storage deployments, and pair this with active thermal management (cabinet cooling, phase-change material, or reduced-SoC scheduling overnight) to keep cell temperature well below 55 °C during idle periods; optionally apply an electrode coating that stabilizes the anode-electrolyte interface to suppress parasitic redox at high anode potentials.
architecture.expected_effect: Substantially slowed calendar-life capacity fade, because lower SOC reduces anode potential-driven electrolyte decomposition and lower cell temperature exponentially suppresses the Arrhenius-rate SEI growth reaction, jointly preserving electrolyte conductivity and limiting SEI thickness accumulation over 36-month storage windows.
architecture.falsification_test: Run two matched sets of LiFePO4/graphite cells at 35 °C/55% SOC versus 55 °C/90% SOC for 12+ months of float, measuring capacity retention and impedance growth; if capacity fade rate at the cooler, lower-SOC condition is not reduced by at least ~50% relative to the hot/high-SOC condition (and SEI thickness does not stay near baseline), the proposed SOC-plus-thermal mitigation is falsified.
